# Class Session 2026-01-27

Session 3 of the [[evening-class-spring-2026|spring 2026 term]], Tuesday 19:00 to 21:00, Carrowmede room 4. Subject: epistolary voice. Thirteen of fourteen students present. The evening that turned Constance Leal's chapters of The Salt Choir into letters.

## At a Glance

> [!note]
> I planned an exercise on letters as documents. Maureen Tighe offered a better one, a letter from a character to the one person they do not perform for, and I wrote one alongside the class in Constance Leal's voice, to her sister Agnes. It came out whole in twenty minutes and did what close third had not. From draft 2 onwards Constance's chapters are letters; Maureen's exercise is credited in my notes as the spark.

## Plan

From [[spring-2026-course-outline]] and [[epistolary-voice-handout-2026-01-27]]:

1. 19:00 to 19:25: what a letter can do that narration cannot. A letter has an addressee, a date and a reason to be written; the writer controls what the reader learns and when. Examples from [[epistolary-novel|the epistolary tradition]] and [[lady-susan|Lady Susan]], which is short enough to describe in a minute.
2. 19:25 to 20:00: my exercise. A letter that also works as evidence: write a letter a character would keep, and one they would burn.
3. Break.
4. 20:15 to 21:00: read-backs and discussion.

## What Happened

During the first half [[maureen-tighe]] said she had used a different letter exercise with teenage readers at her library: write a letter from a character to the one person they do not perform for, and let the reader work out the relationship from the letter alone. The room preferred it, and so did I. After the break we did hers instead of the second half of mine ([[maureen-tighe-letter-exercise]]).

I wrote alongside the class, as I had started doing that term. I chose Constance Leal, who had been flat in the first draft and flatter when I tried her in close third earlier in January. I had her write to her sister Agnes, who never writes back, about the choir. Two sentences of what I wrote that evening, my own draft:

> "I have the altos at last, Agnes, and they are terrible, and I am happier than I have been since Edmund died. Do not tell Mother I said happier."

The rest is in [[constance-sample-letter-2026-01-27]].

Three things happened at once on the page. Constance had an addressee she did not need to perform for, so for the first time she said what she thought. The letter form let her report the town's grief at one remove, which is what a vicar's widow leading the choir would actually do. And the reader could see what she still did not say, which close third had kept spelling out.

## Student Work

Eleven students read back. Under [[student-writing-privacy-rules]] I record only that the strongest pieces came from [[agnieszka-wrona]] (a letter as a list), [[lydia-chen-walsh]] (a letter never sent, from her memoir's period) and [[ronan-maddox]] (a pilot's letter to a ship's master, mostly about tides). No student writing is quoted.

## Decisions And Consequences

- That night: Constance's chapters become letters to her sister. Noted in the draft 2 plan on 2026-02-03 and confirmed on the [[editorial-call-2026-02-19|editorial call of 19 February]] as part of the braided rewrite ([[braided-structure-rewrite]]).
- The letters survived the partial reversal of the braid on [[draft-two-review-2026-07-08|8 July]]: chronology came back, the letters stayed ([[salt-choir-structure-history]]).
- I told Maureen on 2026-02-03 and asked to reuse her exercise with her name on it in later terms. She agreed.
- Writing alongside the class became a habit; my reasons are in [[teaching-feeds-the-writing]].
